sections.h2: Who bills Port St. Lucie property tax
sections.html:
Port St. Lucie lies in St. Lucie County. Three county offices touch your house. The Property Appraiser sets its value, the Tax Collector mails and collects the bill, and the Clerk of Court files your deed. The city adds only its own lines.

The appraiser (paslc.gov) has two offices: Fort Pierce at 2300 Virginia Avenue and Saint Lucie West at 250 NW Country Club Drive. The phone for both is 772-462-1000. The site offers a tax estimator, an online exemption filing portal and homestead portability information. The Tax Collector is at tcslc.com.

  • Property Appraiser: market and assessed value, exemptions, mailing address updates.
  • Tax Collector: bills, discounts, installments, partial payments, delinquent taxes.
  • City of Port St. Lucie: its own millage on the bill, set by the City Council.

The city rate is 4.8750 mills for FY 2026-27, down from 4.9750 the year before. Each mill means a dollar of tax for every thousand of taxable value. The council has trimmed the rate for eleven years running, from 6.6289 in FY 2015/16, a drop of about 25 percent.

The city controls just two lines on your bill: its own rate and the voter-approved debt for the Crosstown Parkway, together about 21 percent of a total bill. The other 14 lines belong to the county, school board, water management district and special districts.

Your bill can still climb when the city rate falls. Taxable value may have risen faster, another authority may have raised its rate, or you may have lost an exemption.

Bills go out on or about November 1. Pay in November and you save 4 percent. The gross amount is due through March 31. Payments received from April 1 onward count as late and carry penalties.

St. Lucie County payment options for Port St. Lucie parcels
Payment optionDates and terms
Early discountNovember 4%, December 3%, January 2%, February 1%, none in March
Partial paymentsUp to 3, minimum $100 each, November through March, no discount
Installment planDue June 30 (6%), September 30 (4.5%), December 30 (3%), March 31 (no discount)
Installment eligibilityApplication closes April 30 of the plan year; estimated tax over $100; current year only

No partial payments are taken after March 31. Applications for the next installment year open each November 1, and past due taxes can't join the plan. Low-income homeowners with homestead can ask about the Homestead Tax Deferral Program, which postpones part of the tax based on household income.

sections.h2: Delinquent taxes and the certificate sale
sections.html:
Miss the March 31 cutoff and the bill is delinquent from April 1, with interest and fees starting. What stays unpaid is offered at the Tax Collector's yearly certificate sale, where bidding opens in May.

To stop a certificate, payment has to be in by five in the evening on the last business day before June 1. Certificates issue on June 1 or the business day after. Online payments shut off at that hour and reopen after processing, usually by mid-June. A payment counts when received, not when postmarked.

  • Accepted forms include cash, cashier's check, money order, wire, credit card, attorney trust check, title company check and mortgage escrow check.
  • The collector can't take partial payments on delinquent taxes, though until a tax deed application is filed they can generally be paid one delinquent year at a time.
  • A certificate doesn't cost you the house, but extra interest and fees apply, and it can later support a tax deed application.

A relative, lender or friend can pay a delinquent bill for you. Doing so gives them no ownership stake.

sections.h2: How a sale changes the tax
sections.html:
Once the deed records, the appraiser is free to reset the house to full just value on the following January 1, and your exemptions don't pass to the new owner. Your exemption and Save Our Homes benefit linger on the parcel through the year of purchase, which is why a buyer's first bill can look gentler than the second.

A buyer who lives in the home on January 1 and files for homestead by March 1 gets the exemption that year, though the cap does not start until the following year. The assessment cap is the lower of 3% or CPI, and the figure is 2.7% for 2026.

Deed stamps run $0.70 per $100 of price. The contract may assign the cost to one side, yet each name on the deed can be pursued for it. The Clerk collects at recording. Ask your closing agent to order the tax payoff and say whether this year's bill is already settled.

Own the home and live in it as of January 1, then apply to the county appraiser before March 1. The first $25,000 applies to every levy including school taxes. The additional exemption reaches non-school taxes only.

Moving within Florida can carry a benefit. Portability lets a mover take up to $500,000 of the Save Our Homes savings to a new homestead. The window is three years, counted from January 1 of the year the old homestead ended.

Extra reductions exist for seniors and for people with disabilities. Homestead ends once the house is rented or stops being your permanent residence, so tell the appraiser instead of waiting for a review.

Look up the parcel on the appraiser's site and confirm that the exemption and value shown are right. Next, collect the Tax Collector's balance for the current year plus any earlier ones, and pass both numbers to the closing agent. If your mailing address changed, update it with the appraiser so notices reach you.

If the bill seems large after a recent reassessment, compare it with the appraiser's tax estimator. TRIM notices show each authority's proposed rate before final rates are certified in the fall. A value dispute goes through the Value Adjustment Board forms on the appraiser's site, and the petition window is 25 days after the TRIM notice goes out.

Owing taxes doesn't block a sale. Your title company or closing agent asks for a payoff figure, and what you owe is deducted from your sale proceeds.

A few simple habits help. Ask for the payoff in writing, and request a fresh one if closing slips. Keep the payoff letter and the final settlement statement together with your sale papers. Tell your agent or buyer about unpaid special assessments or an installment plan still running. A cash buyer skips lender appraisal and underwriting delays, but the tax payoff and deed taxes are settled the same way at the closing table.

faqs.q: Who controls the Port St. Lucie tax rate?
faqs.a: The City Council sets only the city's own rate, 4.8750 mills for FY 2026-27. The county, school board and other authorities set the other lines on your bill.

faqs.q: When do Port St. Lucie taxes go delinquent?
faqs.a: April 1. St. Lucie County bills are due by March 31, and unpaid taxes go into the certificate sale that opens in May.

faqs.q: Does St. Lucie County allow installments?
faqs.a: Yes. The application closes April 30 and the estimated bill must top $100. Expect 6%, 4.5% and 3% discounts on the first three payments.

faqs.q: How do I get the homestead exemption?
faqs.a: File with the St. Lucie County Property Appraiser by March 1, once you own the home and live in it on the January 1 assessment date. The appraiser has an online portal and two offices.

faqs.q: Can a late payment stop a tax certificate?
faqs.a: Only if the Tax Collector has it by five in the evening on the last business day before June 1. A later payment can't stop the certificate, even when mailed earlier.
